frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains reliant on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, creating bargaining leverage but also pressure over pricing, migration, and production expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon investment bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: State dominance protects national control, yet regulatory complexity and aging infrastructure limit foreign investment and constrain long-term production growth.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting major Western and regional interest because of its route to critical minerals, raising concerns about unequal value capture and long-term infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and offshore energy exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain central while debt obligations and foreign participation in offshore projects limit Luanda's room to maximize domestic control over resource income.

frictionVectors.title: Northern border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel threatens transport corridors and agricultural zones, increasing reliance on external security support and regional coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's trade position is closely tied to Nigerian demand and foreign-funded logistics infrastructure, leaving Benin exposed to policy shifts and outside commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana's effort to secure a larger share of diamond sorting, sales, and downstream value strengthens sovereignty but risks commercial friction and reduced investment.

frictionVectors.title: Water and power constraints
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported electricity, regional grids, and scarce water resources limits industrial diversification and creates infrastructure exposure beyond the diamond sector.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent pressure on mining zones
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence threatens gold production, transport routes, and state access in mining regions, making resource sovereignty difficult to enforce outside major urban centers.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining ties
frictionVectors.details: Closer engagement with Russian security networks may reduce Western influence, but opaque arrangements could replace one form of external dependence with another and weaken revenue transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Border Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over rebel support and border insecurity continue to disrupt regional commerce and complicate Burundi's security autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and donors retain substantial leverage over mining, energy, and logistics, while Burundi lacks the capital to capture more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, and other external actors compete for influence around maritime logistics and port modernization, creating dependency risks despite Cabo Verde's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on tourism, imported fuel, and external finance leaves the islands vulnerable to shipping disruptions and outside economic shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Timber, and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign companies and state-linked investors retain strong positions in hydrocarbons, timber, and emerging mining projects, limiting domestic value capture and transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far-North Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the northwest and southwest, alongside Boko Haram-linked threats in the Far North, weakens state control over transport corridors and productive areas.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and politically connected mining interests remain central to regime protection, with access and accountability concerns surrounding resource concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to contest roads, borders, and mining zones, restricting the government's ability to regulate exports or deliver infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to hydrocarbons, export infrastructure, and foreign operators, leaving the state exposed to price volatility and external contractual leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Competition among France, Russia-linked actors, and regional partners shapes counterinsurgency and border policy, while instability in Sudan and Libya strains national control.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros's effective maritime sovereignty and access to surrounding economic resources. The dispute remains a persistent source of diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on foreign financing and contractors. This limits domestic leverage over strategic infrastructure and long-term revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Mineral Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to weaken state control over territory, transport routes, and mineral production. Rwanda-linked security disputes and illicit trade complicate Kinshasa's sovereignty claims.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Contract Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Chinese operators remain deeply embedded in mining, while Western governments seek more secure and transparent critical-mineral supply chains. Weak governance leaves the state with limited bargaining power over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy and public finances remain heavily tied to oil production and foreign energy companies. Limited diversification reduces sovereign resilience when prices, output, or external financing conditions shift.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and urban projects expand connectivity but increase dependence on external capital and contractors. Debt and opaque contracting constrain domestic control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Revenue and Processing Control
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening domestic processing and producer oversight, but international buyers still capture substantial value. Climate stress and volatile prices could undermine these gains.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover Risk
frictionVectors.details: Instability and militant activity near the northern borders pressure security spending and trade routes. Foreign security partnerships remain important, creating a balance between protection and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Base and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through foreign military bases and competing port operators, but this crowds strategic infrastructure with external interests. The government retains leverage while facing pressure from rival powers.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Ethiopian Transit Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port revenues and logistics remain closely tied to Ethiopia's trade, while debt-financed infrastructure creates exposure to foreign creditors. Red Sea insecurity can rapidly disrupt shipping income and national fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water and GERD dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian operation of the GERD, viewing Nile flows as a core national-security issue. Diplomatic engagement remains constrained by the absence of a binding operating agreement.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF requirements and Gulf investment are supporting fiscal stability but increasing outside leverage over major assets, ports, and state-owned enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling production is tightening state revenues and increasing dependence on foreign operators, technical expertise, and regional gas-processing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Malabo offshore and regional gas strategy
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing cross-border gas feedstock and LNG opportunities, creating exposure to foreign capital, maritime competition, and uncertain regional supply commitments.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects remain central to export earnings and rely heavily on external capital and operators, limiting domestic value capture and increasing strategic vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea military competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb attract competing Gulf and wider international interest. Port and security engagement can generate leverage while exposing the country to regional rivalries.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal exposure to SACU transfers
frictionVectors.details: Customs receipts from the Southern African Customs Union remain a major fiscal support, leaving Eswatini vulnerable to South African trade conditions and regional revenue volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and industrial dependence
frictionVectors.details: Energy, logistics, and investment links are concentrated through South Africa and other external partners, constraining policy autonomy but providing relatively stable access to regional infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The dam is expanding Ethiopia's control over domestic power generation and export potential, but its operation remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Port access and regional corridors
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for dependable Red Sea access is driving competition involving Somaliland, Somalia, Djibouti, and external powers. Corridor dependence remains a major constraint on sovereign trade security.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater domestic control over oil, manganese and related infrastructure. This risks friction with established foreign operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export capacity remains dependent on foreign-linked port, rail and mining logistics. Delays in infrastructure reform could limit the state’s leverage over strategic commodities.

highlights: Tourism and fisheries define economic sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and trade exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia remains highly dependent on Senegal for regional access, security coordination and surrounding supply chains. This constrains independent policy while generally supporting stability.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries governance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited enforcement threaten marine-resource control. Weak monitoring can reduce local food security and public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal adjustment and debt-restructuring requirements narrow Accra’s policy space. Recovery depends on restoring market access without surrendering excessive control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining damages land and water while weakening state authority. Emerging interest in lithium and other minerals is increasing competition over licensing, processing and local value addition.

highlights: Junta leverages minerals for state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign-investment concentration
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor is drawing major Chinese and other foreign capital, rail and port commitments. Guinea’s bargaining power is rising, but dependence on external technology and infrastructure remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Transition legitimacy and resource control
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining development to reinforce its authority while delaying a clear return to civilian rule. Political uncertainty increases sovereign and operational risk for investors and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on exporting raw cashews, leaving producers vulnerable to foreign buyers and price swings. Limited domestic processing captures little value.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, trafficking and external influence
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political confrontation undermine control of ports and border networks. Drug-trafficking risks and foreign commercial influence further erode sovereign oversight.

highlights: Ports and critical minerals remain strategic

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and Chinese-financed infrastructure constrain policy flexibility. Nairobi is seeking stronger local control over strategic transport and energy assets while maintaining access to foreign capital.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Lamu corridor attract competing Gulf, Chinese, and Western interests. Regional insecurity and high logistics costs complicate Kenya's effort to turn infrastructure into sovereign economic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues and infrastructure are tightly linked to South Africa, creating fiscal benefits but limiting strategic autonomy. Delays, financing needs, and unequal bargaining power remain persistent concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and textile vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho relies heavily on imported energy and externally controlled export markets, especially for textiles. Any reduction in trade preferences or regional investment would quickly pressure employment and public finances.

highlights: Ports and concessions draw foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore concession leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large mining concessions provide essential revenue and jobs but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and difficult negotiations over royalties, local processing, and infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign management and investment in ports, roads, and logistics are necessary for growth but can narrow the government's control over strategic gateways. Weak institutional capacity increases the risk of opaque or unbalanced agreements.

highlights: Oil remains divided by rival authorities

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and revenue distribution. Foreign firms and governments retain leverage through contracts, technical dependence, and political relationships.

frictionVectors.title: External military footprint
frictionVectors.details: Rival foreign-backed security relationships complicate national reunification and expose energy infrastructure to coercion. The absence of unified security institutions weakens Libya's control over its territorial and resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects generate exports and infrastructure but remain heavily dependent on foreign capital, technology, and offtake arrangements. Madagascar faces pressure to capture more processing value and enforce environmental obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Rare earth and port competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in rare earths and coastal infrastructure is increasing among Asian and Western investors. Weak transport networks and regulatory uncertainty make the state vulnerable to concession terms that prioritize extraction over domestic industrial development.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led mineral expansion
frictionVectors.details: Renewed interest in uranium, rare earths and other minerals could bring investment, but weak state capacity limits Malawi's ability to secure high domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and electricity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported fuel and fragile hydropower leaves the country vulnerable to external price shocks and climate-driven supply disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-code confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The state is demanding larger shares from gold projects, creating friction with foreign operators while operational uncertainty threatens investment and production.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-resources exposure
frictionVectors.details: Deepening ties with Russian security providers increase dependence on an external power and complicate relations with regional and Western partners.

highlights: Gas exports begin to reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractive infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas and iron-ore projects rely heavily on international operators, financing and logistics, limiting near-term domestic control despite rising state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail and energy infrastructure is becoming a focus of Gulf, European and Chinese interest, creating leverage opportunities but also exposure to external agendas.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty transition
frictionVectors.details: The future of the Chagos Archipelago and the Diego Garcia base remains central to Mauritius's sovereignty claims and its relationship with Britain, the United States and India.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in energy and food
frictionVectors.details: As a small island economy, Mauritius remains exposed to imported fuel, food and shipping costs despite strong institutions and diversified services.

frictionVectors.title: European energy and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding solar, wind, green-hydrogen and industrial capacity, but remains exposed to European markets, imported energy inputs and external project finance.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and infrastructure linked to Western Sahara continue to generate legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front and European partners.

highlights: Cabo Delgado insurgency constrains LNG revival

frictionVectors.title: LNG project security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence and weak local security capacity continue to delay major gas development. International operators retain substantial leverage over financing, security arrangements, and project timelines.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Maputo, Nacala, and Beira corridors remain vital but vulnerable to external ownership, regional competition, and uneven state oversight.

highlights: Green hydrogen diplomacy expands strategic autonomy
Uranium and offshore oil attract competing partners

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Namibia is using licensing and local-content rules to seek greater value from uranium, lithium, and emerging oil resources. Foreign capital remains essential, creating tension over ownership and downstream processing.

frictionVectors.title: Green hydrogen infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large projects depend on European, Gulf, and Asian finance and offtake agreements. The government is seeking sovereign control without slowing development through excessive external conditionality.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and hydrocarbons
Sanctions and insecurity isolate supply routes

frictionVectors.title: Resource nationalism versus investment
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating foreign mining and energy relationships to increase state control, but political uncertainty and sanctions restrict technical capacity and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Landlocked export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Border closures, militant threats, and dependence on neighboring transit states complicate uranium, oil, and agricultural exports. Alternative partnerships have not yet produced reliable infrastructure.

highlights: Dangote refining strengthens domestic energy leverage
Oil theft and grid weakness erode gains

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and production decline
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is seeking more local refining and processing while still relying on international firms, technology, and financing to sustain upstream output and gas development.

frictionVectors.title: Energy infrastructure insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and unreliable electricity continue to reduce the state’s effective control over strategic energy assets and weaken fiscal returns.

highlights: Mineral trading boosts Kigali’s regional leverage
Eastern Congo tensions sharpen sovereignty risks

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes mineral scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda’s role in regional mineral supply chains faces sustained international scrutiny amid allegations that conflict-linked resources transit through its territory. Diplomatic pressure threatens access to premium markets and aid relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Security partnerships and dependency
frictionVectors.details: External security cooperation and regional deployments provide influence and revenue, but they also expose Kigali to conditionality, sanctions risk, and reputational costs.

frictionVectors.title: Exploration and revenue uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Deepwater exploration has yet to deliver commercially proven reserves, leaving the country reliant on external capital and vulnerable to unfavorable future production-sharing terms.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak port, energy, and maritime-security capacity increases dependence on outside partners, including China and other foreign investors, for strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New hydrocarbon revenues strengthen Dakar's leverage, but pressure to revise legacy contracts and increase local content could unsettle foreign operators and financing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign fishing continue to strain coastal livelihoods, while offshore energy development creates additional competition over marine space and enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, ports, and infrastructure depend heavily on external capital, creating recurring concerns over debt exposure, land access, and the long-term control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal fishing and maritime surveillance
frictionVectors.details: The country's vast exclusive economic zone is difficult to monitor, leaving fisheries vulnerable and requiring security and surveillance support from India, France, and other partners.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore and mineral projects generate export revenue but leave fiscal stability and infrastructure development exposed to commodity prices and foreign operating partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and land pressure
frictionVectors.details: Road, rail, and port investments linked to mining can improve connectivity, yet land access, environmental safeguards, and weak domestic processing continue to limit sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port competition and foreign security influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, and other partners compete for influence over ports, logistics, and security arrangements, complicating federal control of strategic maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resources and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil, gas, and fisheries resources remain difficult to govern because of insecurity, federal-regional tensions, and limited maritime enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, rail capacity, and port congestion constrain sovereign control over mineral value chains. Foreign mining, trading, and infrastructure partners remain important, while policy uncertainty limits new investment.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic alignment pressure
frictionVectors.details: South Africa balances BRICS ties, Western trade and finance, and regional security responsibilities. Competing external expectations increasingly affect decisions on critical minerals, technology, and sanctions.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on foreign operators and Sudanese export infrastructure to monetize its oil, leaving revenues vulnerable to war, pipeline disruption, and opaque bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized security economy
frictionVectors.details: Regional governments, foreign security networks, and aid providers retain substantial leverage amid unresolved political and ethnic tensions. Weak transport infrastructure further limits independent state reach.

highlights: Gold and ports become strategic prizes

frictionVectors.title: Competing external sponsors
frictionVectors.details: The conflict has deepened reliance on outside arms, finance, and political backing, while gold networks and border trade help sustain rival power centers.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime facilities, and transport corridors are increasingly tied to foreign strategic interests. Damage and insecurity around national infrastructure further reduce sovereign economic control.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, energy, and logistics projects bring stronger regional connectivity but also increase exposure to Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing interests. Contract transparency and local-value concerns remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater domestic processing and state participation in mining, but foreign capital and technical capacity remain essential. Disputes over revenue sharing and community benefits could test the policy shift.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port and logistics economy provide regional influence but depend heavily on foreign operators, finance, and cross-border trade flows. Disruptions in the Sahel could weaken transit revenues and security.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate production and emerging extractive projects remain exposed to commodity cycles and external technology. The government retains formal control, but local value addition and oversight capacity are limited.

frictionVectors.title: EU financing and migration conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European support for budget stability and migration management gives Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Tunisia is resisting formalized migration-hosting expectations while remaining financially dependent on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and electricity vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy production and reliance on Algerian gas and electricity limit Tunisia's strategic room for maneuver. Delays in renewable-energy investment increase exposure to external supply and financing conditions.

highlights: Oil corridor locks in regional leverage

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline is advancing under Chinese-led financing and construction support, while European banks and activists continue to oppose or scrutinize the project. The dispute exposes Uganda to reputational, financial, and diplomatic pressure over environmental and human-rights concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a strong position in roads, power, and extractive investment, while Gulf and Western actors seek greater access to minerals and logistics. Uganda is attempting to preserve bargaining power but remains dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Copper and critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using its copper and cobalt endowment to attract Gulf, Chinese, American, and European investment while seeking more local processing. Competition improves negotiating leverage, but foreign ownership, tax disputes, and infrastructure dependence remain persistent risks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved macroeconomic credibility but constrains public investment and requires continued engagement with official and private creditors. Rail, power, and export routes remain vulnerable to financing gaps and regional bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-control measures and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Harare is promoting domestic processing and tighter control over lithium, platinum, and gold, but the sector remains reliant on Chinese and other foreign investors for capital, equipment, and market access. Policy unpredictability and allegations of opaque deals weaken the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, currency instability, and energy shortages
frictionVectors.details: Targeted Western sanctions and weak access to concessional finance continue to raise transaction costs and limit infrastructure investment. Currency instability and unreliable electricity further reduce Zimbabwe's bargaining power with external mining and energy partners.
